rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while revealing the usable elution window and whether late peaks are trapped at high retention. This balances coverage and runtime so the first run is informative for setting a tighter phi window and adjusting slope on the next injection.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only way to improve CRF is to pull the last peak under 10 minutes without losing resolution. The first run shows the compounds elute over roughly phi_e 0.09 to 0.38, so a tighter and slightly stronger gradient window with a shorter tG should keep all peaks in-gradient while cutting t_last substantially.

Resolution still has full credit, so push for speed: a shorter gradient and higher temperature should bring the last peak below 10 minutes. Raising phi1 slightly helps ensure the latest compound does not linger on the hold while keeping the window close to the observed elution range.

The only score loss is the 6/7 pair, which collapsed when the gradient was made steeper and hotter. Backing off temperature slightly and making the gradient a bit shallower should recover that pair's resolution while likely keeping the last peak under 10 minutes.

The 6/7 pair is highly temperature-selective: at 50 C it was much better than at 45 C, while all runs show enough speed to stay below 10 minutes if we keep the method fairly strong. Narrowing the window slightly versus run 3 and using an intermediate slope should test whether that pair can be brought back above 1.5 without sacrificing the zero time penalty.

The difficult 6/7 pair appears more sensitive to the phi window than to slope alone: it was best at 40 C with the broadest window and worsened when the window was tightened. Shift the whole gradient slightly stronger while keeping it short enough to preserve t_last under 10 minutes, aiming to move that pair into a more selective part of the gradient.

The best 6/7 resolution so far came from the broadest, coolest window, suggesting this pair benefits from lower effective phi rather than from a tighter or hotter method. Keep the fast 8 minute gradient to preserve the zero time penalty, but broaden and shift the window weaker to try to recover selectivity for the critical pair.

The critical pair improved most at higher temperature, while changes to the phi window have mostly hurt selectivity. Test whether the broad original window combined with the fast 8 minute gradient and 50 C can keep the run under 10 minutes yet move the 6/7 pair into a more favorable selectivity region than the tighter-window fast methods.

The broad window at 50 C is currently best, and the remaining loss is confined to the compact central cluster. A slightly shallower gradient should improve the 4/5 and especially 6/7 resolutions while likely keeping t_last comfortably below 10 minutes.

At 50 C with the broad window, increasing tG from 8 to 10 min did not hurt runtime and kept full time credit, so one more step shallower is worth testing. The only remaining score loss is the 6/7 pair, and if it responds at all to slope this should improve it while still leaving ample margin below 10 minutes for the last peak.

The broad window is clearly best, and the critical 6/7 pair improved moving from 40 to 50 C at comparable fast slopes. A higher temperature is the most promising remaining lever for selectivity while t_last at the current optimum leaves enough margin to stay under 10 minutes.

At 55 C the problematic pair shifted from 6/7 to 4/5, indicating temperature helped the former and changed the local selectivity of the central cluster. A slightly steeper gradient may open 4/5 while still keeping all peaks well under 10 minutes on this broad, successful window.

At 55 C the limiting pair is now 4/5, and making the gradient steeper hurt it badly, so the next test should go shallower rather than steeper. There is plenty of time margin below 10 minutes, so tG 12 min is a safe way to see whether 4/5 gains enough spacing without sacrificing the good 6/7 resolution.

The optimum has already been reached, so any new run can only check robustness near the best point. A slightly shallower version of the winning method should remain fully resolved and under 10 minutes while confirming the plateau around the maximum.

You already have a perfect method, so this run should map the local robustness boundary in the remaining temperature direction. Testing 60 C at the winning slope checks whether higher temperature still preserves full resolution while keeping the run comfortably under 10 minutes.

The best point is already known, so this run should probe robustness in phi0 near the optimum. Raising phi0 slightly while keeping the winning tG and T tests whether the fully resolved window is broad or whether early-gradient composition is critical to maintaining the perfect separation.

The perfect point appears somewhat sensitive to phi0 and temperature, so now probe the upper end of the gradient window instead. Lowering phi1 slightly while keeping the winning tG and T tests whether the latest compound still stays in-gradient and whether the central selectivity remains fully resolved.

You now have a second perfect method, so the best use of another run is to see whether the same narrowed upper window can be made faster without losing full resolution. Shortening tG by one step should test whether this robust region extends toward a shorter cycle time while staying under the 10 minute last-peak limit.

The narrowed phi1=0.90 window also reaches CRF 1.000 at tG 12, so a slightly shallower version usefully maps the robustness boundary on the slow side. This tests whether the perfect region extends upward in tG for the 0.90 endpoint or whether the 6/7 pair starts to slip below full credit.

You have mapped that phi1 0.90–0.95 at 12 min and 55 C is optimal, so the next useful robustness check is one more step lower in phi1. This tests how sharply the perfect region ends at the high-organic endpoint while keeping the proven winning slope and temperature.

The phi1 boundary is turning out to be close to the optimum, with 0.85 just missing full credit and 0.90–0.95 perfect. One more step lower in phi1 will define that edge more clearly while holding the proven best tG and temperature constant.

This continues the phi1 robustness map at the winning tG and T, and the trend so far suggests the limiting 6/7 pair slowly weakens as phi1 decreases. One more step to 0.75 should define that boundary better while remaining safely within the observed elution range.

You already know the optimum and most nearby failures, so a useful remaining check is a combined edge case on the slower and lower-phi1 side of the robust region. This should clarify whether the near-perfect phi1=0.85 method loses full credit mainly from reduced phi1, increased tG, or their interaction.

With only two injections left and the optimum already found, the best remaining value is to map the lower temperature boundary for the second perfect window at phi1 0.90. This isolates the effect of dropping temperature without also changing the broader phi1 0.95 window, helping define how narrowly 55 C is required for full resolution.

For the final run, probe the fast-side edge of the near-optimal phi1=0.85 window to complete the local map around the best region. This will show whether the small loss at phi1=0.85 is mainly from endpoint choice or whether a shorter gradient shifts the limiting pair toward the same 4/5 behavior seen at faster perfect-window methods.
